We found that higher amygdala activity was predictive of both in-scanner ratings of quit intentions (β = 0.078, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.001–0.157) and population information seeking (β = 0.099, 95% CI = 0.020–0.174) across the negatively valenced anti-smoking messages.

The results of this model ( Fig. 2 ) indicated that the relationship between amygdala activity and quit intentions was mediated by vmPFC activity, a * b quit_int = 0.044, 95% CI = 0.017–0.074) and, similarly, the relationship between amygdala activity and population information seeking was also mediated by vmPFC activity ( a * b pop_beh = 0.038, 95% CI = 0.005–0.073).

This pattern is consistent with a model whereby amygdala responses reflect bottom-up affective reactivity to an emotionally evocative anti-smoking message and this bottom-up reactivity is predictive of individual- and population-level message effects to the extent that it tracks with corresponding valuation-related responses in vmPFC.

Within the neutral comparison messages, we did not see mediation by vmPFC for either quit intentions ( a * b = 0.020, 95% CI = −0.011 to 0.051) or population information seeking ( a * b = −0.051, 95% CI = −0.013 to 0.025). Overall, this pattern of results is consistent with a model whereby amygdala responses reflect bottom-up affective reactivity to an emotionally evocative anti-smoking message and this bottom-up reactivity is predictive of individual- and population-level message effects to the extent that it tracks with corresponding valuation-related responses in vmPFC.
